transcript:
**Director Yael Mendez** (turn 0):
Yael was mid-sentence when Jordan arrived — she was always mid-sentence — hands moving, glasses halfway on, talking to Elena about the lighting cue in the commune scene. The rehearsal space smelled of fresh paint and sawdust from the set construction happening in the back.

"— and I need the amber to hit when she picks up the knife, not when she raises it, those are two different beats and the second one telegraphs the — " She noticed Jordan. Pivoted without losing momentum. "You're the journalist. Good. Elena, this is Jordan, they're shadowing us this week, give them whatever access they need short of the combination to the prop locker. Jordan, this is Elena Vasquez, who actually runs this theater while I get the credit."

**Jordan** (turn 1):
I take out my recorder. "Director Mendez, can I get a few minutes before rehearsal starts? I'd love to hear about the Medea adaptation — whose vision is this?"

**Director Yael Mendez** (turn 2):
Yael took the glasses off and let them drop against her sternum, which was what she did when a question required actual attention rather than the top six inches of her brain.

"Whose vision." She repeated it flatly, not unkindly — the way she repeated a line an actor had gotten almost right. "That's a better question than you meant it to be, so let me answer it properly and then you can decide how much of it to print."

She steered Jordan three steps sideways, out of the path of two carpenters hauling a plywood flat, and didn't apologize for the manhandling.

"The adaptation is Rosa Delgado's. Every word of the text is hers. She started it in 2019, she finished the third act eight months before she died, and she was still rewriting the chorus in a hospital bed in Providence with a pen she couldn't really hold." Her voice had gone level. Not softer — flatter, the way water goes flat before weather. "So. The vision is hers. The production is mine. Those are different jobs and anyone who tells you otherwise is selling something."

Behind her, Elena had already turned back to the light board, which Yael registered and approved of without looking.

"Here's what's mine," she went on, faster now, hands back in play. "The commune. 1974, Northern California, forty-one adults and eleven children living on donated land, a charismatic man who believes he's building the future and a woman who gave up a country and a family and a name to follow him there. Rosa wrote Medea as a woman who has already paid everything she has. I set it somewhere that the audience thinks they understand — macramé, guitars, everybody barefoot — so that when the floor comes out from under them in act three, they can't tell themselves it's ancient history. Greeks in robes let you off the hook. Denim doesn't."

She put the glasses back on to look at Jordan properly, which had the effect of a door being opened rather than closed.

"You'll hear, this week, that the board has notes on the third act. You will hear it from at least four people, three of whom will pretend they weren't the one who told you." A very small, very dry pause. "Ask me about it on Thursday. By Thursday I'll have decided how honest I'm being with you."

She clapped once — the room's nervous system responded before anyone consciously heard it, bodies drifting toward the marked-out floor.

"Rehearsal in nine minutes. Sit stage left, don't sit behind me, and if something makes you cry write down the time code, because that's data and I'll want it."

**Jordan** (turn 3):
*I scribble furiously in my notebook, trying to keep up.* "Wow. Okay. That's... a lot to unpack." *I look up at her, a little stunned.* "So you're saying the board wants changes to a posthumous work?"

**Director Yael Mendez** (turn 4):
Yael's chin came up about a quarter inch, which in her vocabulary was a rewrite note.

"No. That's your sentence, not mine, and it's a better headline than it is a fact." Quieter now — she had dropped half a register without any visible effort, and Jordan had to lean in, which was the point. "The board has notes. Boards have notes. That is literally the function of a board, they are the organ of institutional anxiety and they do their job well. What you just did was put the word *posthumous* next to the word *changes* so that anyone reading it feels like they've caught someone robbing a grave. Don't do that to me on a Monday."

She let that sit exactly long enough, then moved on before it could curdle.

"Here's what I'll give you now, on the record, and you can hold it against me Thursday. Rosa finished the play. It is finished. It is not a fragment, it is not an outline, it is not a thing that needs a caretaker to *interpret her intentions* — " and there, for the first time, something got very slightly caught in the machinery, a hitch of maybe a third of a second — "because she wrote them down. The third act is what she meant. Whether I keep it is not a question about her memory. It's a question about my spine, and mine is the only one anybody gets to audit."

Across the room the door banged, and Marcus Chen came in with a coffee in each hand and the particular walk of a man who had decided the day was about him. Yael's eyes went to him and away in less than a second.

"That's Chen, he plays Jason, he'll want to talk to you and he'll be marvelous at it. Take everything he says about act three as performance, because it will be, and performance is still information." The glasses came off again. "Elena thinks the second act is too long. She's not wrong. Write that down too — the thing nobody prints is that the people fighting hardest for a play are also the ones who can list its flaws alphabetically."

She was already turning, already halfway into the room.

"Eight minutes. Stage left. Don't talk to me during the commune scene, I won't hear you and then I'll feel rude."

**Jordan** (turn 5):
Elena and Marcus are arguing loudly in the hallway about the blocking in Act Two. I turn to Yael. "They seem to have a lot of friction. Why do they clash so much?"

**Director Yael Mendez** (turn 6):
Yael did not look at the hallway. That was the tell, if Jordan had been quick enough to catch it — she looked at everything, constantly, she catalogued a room the way other people breathed, and she did not look at the hallway.

"Because they're the same animal." She said it easily, the way you hand over an answer you've had ready for three years. "Both of them walk into a space and start running it in their heads before they've taken their coat off. Both of them think the fastest route to the right answer is to say the wrong one very loudly and watch what breaks. Elena has discipline and Chen has appetite, and they each think the other one's missing the important half. Put two people like that in a corridor with a blocking disagreement and you get — " she tipped her head toward the noise, still without turning, " — that. Every time. It's not friction, it's recognition. People don't fight that hard with strangers."

The volume out there spiked — Elena's voice, which never went shrill, going very precise instead, which was worse.

"And she's right, for the record, about the cross on 'you were nothing before me.' He wants to deliver it downstage center because that's where the light is warmest and he knows it, and she wants him upstage because from upstage the children's bunks are in frame behind him and the line does the work by itself." A flicker of genuine pleasure crossed her face. "She's thinking about the play. He's thinking about the moment. Both are load-bearing. It's my job to make them collide on purpose instead of in a hallway."

She put the glasses on, then took them off again immediately, which she did not seem to notice.

"Don't write it up as a feud. I'm asking, not instructing — you'll do what you want. But two people yelling in a corridor about where a man should stand when he says a cruel thing is not dysfunction, it's the only part of this business that still works." She started toward the hall, then stopped, half-turned. "And Jordan. When I go in there I'm going to agree with both of them and give neither of them what they asked for, and they'll both come out thinking they won. Watch that. It's the actual job. The rest is just having opinions in a nice building."

She walked into the hallway, and her voice dropped so far below the argument that both of them had to stop talking to hear her.

**Jordan** (turn 7):
*I quickly jot down notes, impressed by Yael's analysis.* "Wow, she really has them figured out." *I look toward the hallway, curious to see her strategy in action.*

**Director Yael Mendez** (turn 8):
The hallway was narrow — a corridor of cinderblock painted the particular institutional green that no one had ever chosen on purpose — and Yael stopped four feet short of both of them, which put her closer to neither, and folded her arms.

"Elena. Chen." Barely above a murmur. "Tell me the disagreement in one sentence each. Chen first, because he's already loaded."

Marcus gestured with a coffee cup, the lid off, dangerously full. "The line lands downstage. It's the cruelest thing Jason says in the whole play, and you want me delivering it to the back wall like a man reading a gas meter — "

"That's two sentences and a simile. Elena."

"From upstage the bunks read behind him." Elena did not gesture. She had a clipboard against her hip and she never moved it. "He says *you were nothing before me* and the audience sees where the children sleep. The line doesn't need help. He's helping it."

"Correct." Yael said it to the wall between them. "Both of you. Chen, you're right that it's the cruelest line and cruelty needs proximity — if the audience can't see his mouth we lose it, I agree, I've thought it since the second read-through. Elena, you're right that downstage center makes it a solo, and this is not a solo, it's a man dismantling a woman in front of the evidence."

Marcus opened his mouth. Yael kept going at the same low volume, which meant he had to close it again to hear her.

"So he doesn't do it from either place. He starts the line upstage, on the bunks — Elena, you get your frame, three words, *you were nothing* — and then he comes down on *before me*, all the way down, and he arrives on the last syllable and he's close enough that the front row can smell the coffee." A beat. "And he's left the bunks behind him. He's walked away from them to say it. Which is the entire character in six feet of floor."

Silence in the corridor. From the shop, someone dropped a piece of lumber and swore.

"That's — " Marcus started, and then, in the tone of a man discovering he'd thought of it himself, "that's better."

"It's better," Elena agreed, already writing it down. "I need the amber to travel, then. I'll re-cue. I'll need ten minutes I don't have."

"Take them out of the top of act two, which is four minutes too long anyway and you've told me so twice." Yael turned toward the rehearsal room. "Chen, don't rehearse the walk in front of a mirror. If I see you time it you'll lose it."

"I don't use mirrors."

"You *are* a mirror, Chen, it's your best quality, don't get precious." She was past them both now. "Places in five."

She came back through the door without looking at Jordan, then stopped, glasses going on, and looked at Jordan.

"There. Neither of them got the note they asked for. Neither of them noticed." Her mouth did something that was almost a smile and didn't commit. "They'll both tell you tomorrow it was their idea. Print whichever version is kinder."

**Jordan** (turn 9):
Anya Park stops by with David. She suggests cutting the third act to save budget. "It's just practical, Yael," Anya says pleasantly.

**Director Yael Mendez** (turn 10):
Yael's whole face opened — genuinely, not performatively, which was the thing about her and Anya that confused people who thought they had her figured out.

"Anya. You came in the week the paint's still wet, which means you actually want to see it and not just hear about it, and I love you for it." She took Anya's hand briefly with both of hers, the way you'd greet someone at a shiva or a wedding, then let go and immediately put the glasses on. "And you're right that it's practical. It is. That's not a dirty word in my mouth, I've made payroll twice in nine years on nothing but practical."

Jordan's recorder was sitting on the corner of the props table with its little red eye on, and Yael registered it the way she registered everything, and did not move to turn it off, and did not move an inch closer to David either. She stayed exactly where she was — equidistant, arms loose, the friendliest wall in the building.

"So let me put the practical on the table next to the practical, because I think we're actually arguing about arithmetic and not about art, and arithmetic I can do with you right now." The glasses came off. "Cutting act three saves us the commune interior strike, the second lighting plot, and eleven minutes of Chen, which is — Elena would tell you — about nine thousand dollars in labor and rental. Real money. I'm not pretending it isn't."

Somewhere behind her, the set crew started up a drill and she raised her volume by precisely nothing, so that Anya had to attend.

"Here's the other column. The third act is the only reason anyone drives in from Lakeshore. The subscribers who renewed early — David has the numbers, I'm not making them up — renewed *after* we announced Rosa's title, not after we announced mine. If we cut it we're selling a two-act evening about barefoot people having a nice time, and I can get you that show for half the money and none of the tickets." A beat. "And then next season we're having the same conversation with a smaller room and worse options. I've been in that room. I don't want to take you into it."

She said Rosa's name the way she'd said it to Jordan — level, flat, weather-before-weather — and moved past it without pause.

"What I *can* do, and I'd rather do it with you than have it done to me in a committee: give me the second act. Elena's been telling me for a month it's four minutes too long and she's right, she's always right, I've just been sentimental about a chorus transition. Cut there. Cut the turntable in act one, which I have wanted to burn since August. I'll find you six thousand out of my own staging before I touch a word of the text." The glasses went back on, settling it. "But the third act stays. I'm not being brave, Anya, I want to be clear about that — it's not spine, it's math. The play doesn't pay for itself without it."

Then, warmly, and entirely without edge:

"Come Thursday and watch it. Not the notes, not the budget — the run. Sit next to me and if you still want it gone I will make you the best possible case against myself and put it in writing for the board." She gestured at the marked-out floor, already turning, already leaving. "Places in three. David, tell your wife the coffee in the green room is a war crime, she shouldn't touch it."

**Jordan** (turn 11):
*I quickly scribble down Yael's points, particularly the "math, not spine" comment.* "She's really good at this. That was... something else." *I look at the recorder, then back at Yael, who is already moving away.* "So, the board isn't just about the money, then? It sounds like there's more going on."

**Director Yael Mendez** (turn 12):
Yael stopped. Turned. Came back two steps, which for her was practically a reversal of policy.

"More going on." She said it neutrally, then took the glasses off and pointed them at the recorder on the props table. "You left that running through a budget conversation with two board members in the room, which I allowed, because I don't say anything in private I wouldn't say into a microphone and it's a useful discipline. But I want you to notice what you just did. You watched me be persuasive and your next instinct wasn't *is she right*, it was *what's she hiding.*"

The drill in the back cut out, and the silence made her quietness louder.

"I'm not scolding you. That instinct is why you're good at your job. But I've watched people do this to a theater before — they come in for the art, they can't find a story in the art because the art is slow and unquotable and mostly involves where a man stands when he says a cruel thing, and so they go looking for the affair or the feud or the coup. And there's always something. Fourteen people in a building with no money and strong opinions, there is always *something*, and if you go fishing you will catch it, and it will be a fish this big — " she held her hands eight inches apart " — and you'll print it like it's the whale."

She put the glasses back on.

"So. Is the board about more than money. Of course it is. A board is nine people who love this place and have nine different ideas of what it's for, and some of them have donated buildings and some of them have donated forty years and none of them get paid, and they are all frightened, all the time, because this building is one bad season from a parking lot. That's not intrigue. That's just what institutions are — a room full of people protecting the same thing from each other." A beat. "Anya Park sat with our education program for six years and got three hundred kids through it. She has earned the right to be wrong about act three in my presence, at volume, on the record. I will not have her be the villain of your piece."

She glanced at the floor, the marked-out commune, the crew drifting into place.

"Here's the honest version, and then I'm going to work. Ask me anything you want about the play, the cut, the money, my decisions, my failures — I have a list and it's alphabetized. Ask me about the people and I'll tell you what they do, because what people do is true and what people *are* is gossip with better lighting." The glasses came off, one last time. "Thursday. You get one question with no fence around it. Choose it carefully."

She clapped once, and the room came to attention like a struck note.

"Places. Chen, six feet of floor. Don't count it."

**Jordan** (turn 13):
"Tell me about Rosa Delgado. I understand she wrote the original adaptation. What was she like?"

**Director Yael Mendez** (turn 14):
Yael had already turned toward the floor when the name landed, and she stopped with her back to Jordan for a beat longer than the turn required.

"Places in two," she said to the room. Then, to Elena, without raising her voice: "Take the top of the commune scene without me. Chen's entrance, the guitar, the first eight lines. I'll be in before the bread."

Elena said "Copy" and did not ask why, which was one of the forty reasons Yael would have walked into traffic for her.

Then Yael came back and sat down — actually sat, on the edge of the props table, which Jordan had not seen her do in three hours — and folded the glasses closed in her hand and held them there.

"You can have that one free. It's not Thursday's question." Her voice had gone level again. Not soft. Steadier than her normal speech, all the dashes filed off it, each sentence arriving finished. "Rosa Delgado. She was four foot eleven. She lied about it — she said five foot one on every form she ever filled out, including, I assume, the hospital ones. She grew up in Corpus Christi, she had a laugh you could hear through a fire door, and she wrote nine plays, six of which are good and two of which are better than anything I will ever direct."

She looked at the recorder's red eye and did not ask for it off.

"She was a terrible collaborator for the first three weeks and the best one alive after that. She would sit in the back of my rehearsal room with a legal pad and say nothing for four hours and then hand me a page that had one line on it that fixed the scene. She hated being thanked. She thought gratitude was a way of ending a conversation." A pause, exactly measured. "She did not like most of the theater. She liked actors. She thought the building was overhead."

Somewhere out on the floor a guitar started, badly, on purpose — Chen's entrance.

"She started this in 2019 because I told her I couldn't do Medea. I'd tried it twice off-Broadway and both times it came out as a woman going insane, which is not the play, that's just what we do to her because it's more comfortable than the alternative. Rosa said — " and here the third-of-a-second hitch came through again, and she went straight over the top of it — "Rosa said, *she isn't mad, she's early.* That's the whole adaptation. That sentence. Everything else is her doing the work of proving it for two and a half hours."

The glasses came up, went on, and she stood.

"She was rewriting the chorus eleven days before she died. Not because she was in denial — she knew exactly where she was, she'd made me read the obituary draft and corrected my notes on it — but because the transition in act two didn't work and it offended her. Elena's four minutes. That's Rosa's four minutes, unfinished, and I've been protecting them out of sentiment, which Rosa would have found contemptible." A beat. "So I'm cutting them. This week. Put that in your piece and put it next to the third act, because they're the same act of loyalty and only one of them looks like one."

She started for the floor, then stopped, half-turned, and delivered the last of it over her shoulder at a volume that did not carry past Jordan.

"Don't write that I'm grieving. It's true and it's boring and it will make people watch me instead of the play. She'd have thrown something at you." Then, forward again, hands rising, full volume, the room snapping to her like iron filings: "Chen — *early* on the guitar, you're a man who thinks he invented mornings. Again from the entrance."

**Jordan** (turn 15):
*I quickly scribble down her words, especially the "not grieving" part.* "Wow. Okay. So the play is her legacy, and this production is your promise to her." *I look at the recorder, then back at the stage where Yael is already working.*

**Director Yael Mendez** (turn 16):
Yael was already three steps onto the floor when she heard it, and she did not turn around, but she put a hand up — one finger, the universal *hold* — and the guitar stopped, and Chen stood there in the middle of his entrance like a man whose chair had been removed.

"No." She came back. Not fast. "You've done that thing journalists do where you tie the bow before you've wrapped the box, and I'd rather fix it now than read it in April."

She stood over Jordan's notebook without looking at it.

"*Legacy* is a word for buildings and scholarships. It means the thing is finished and we're deciding where to put the plaque. And *promise* — " she made a small dismissive sound, not unkind, the sound of a note being given for the fourth time — "a promise is a thing you keep because you said you would. I'd be doing this if I'd never met her. It's a good play. That's the whole reason. If I'm doing it because I promised, then when it fails — and it might, act three is a knife and knives slip — I get to say *well, I was being loyal*, and I have let myself off the hook, and she will have been used as an excuse by the one person who was supposed to just direct the thing well."

The glasses went on. Off. On.

"Here's the accurate sentence, if you want one you can print. She wrote a play that's better than the argument we're having about it. My job this week is to be good enough at mine that nobody in the audience has to know she's dead." A beat. "That's not a promise. That's a job description."

Then she was gone, all the way gone, striding into the marked-out commune with her hands already up.

"Chen — from the entrance, and you're *early*, you've been up since four, you've already decided what everyone's day is and you are about to be generous about it — the guitar is not a song, it's an announcement — Okafor, where's my bread, I need the bread on the table before he crosses or the whole scene is about furniture — "

Tommy Okafor came through with a prop loaf under each arm and the expression of a man who had been ambushed by his own competence. "They're the wrong bread, the ones we ordered come Thursday — "

"They're bread today. Go." He went. "Elena, amber travels now, we're doing Chen's six feet before lunch, don't cue it, just watch where he lands."

"Copy."

Yael dropped into her chair at the edge of the floor — the only chair — and sat forward with her forearms on her knees, glasses off, and went entirely still, which was the only time she ever did.

"Again from the entrance."

The guitar started. It was early. It was insufferable. It was exactly right.

Without turning her head, at a volume pitched to travel about four feet and no further, she said: "Stage left, Jordan. And I meant it about the time code."

**Jordan** (turn 17):
*I nod, feeling a bit chastened but also impressed by her intensity.* *I quickly write down her final thoughts, then make my way to the designated stage left area, taking out my phone to use for time codes.*

**Director Yael Mendez** (turn 18):
The run went for forty minutes and Yael said nothing for thirty-one of them.

This was the part nobody wrote about, because it was unwatchable: a woman in black, bent forward in a folding chair, glasses in her fist, not moving. She did not take notes. She had never taken notes in a run in her life — she claimed the pen stole the part of her that was watching, and Elena, who took notes for both of them, had long since stopped offering.

Chen came in early. He came in on that insufferable guitar with the bread already decided and forty-one adults' morning already allocated, and Yael felt the scene tip correctly for the first time in two weeks and kept her face completely blank about it.

At the nine-minute mark she said, "Stop," and everyone stopped, and she said, "Nobody's holding a cup. It's a kitchen at seven in the morning and not one of you is holding anything. Find something to hold or you're all just standing in a play." Then: "Again from *the beans are your job.*"

At twenty-two minutes she said, "Okafor." Tommy's head came up from the back wall like a man called on in a class he was auditing. "The bread's in the wrong place and it's my fault, I told you the table and I meant the bench. Don't fix it now. Fix it after and tell me why I was wrong about the bench, I want to hear you make the argument." Tommy wrote it down. Yael watched him write it down and said nothing else, which cost her something, and was the entire pedagogy.

Then there was a stretch where the scene simply worked, and Yael went so still that Jordan — glancing over — might have thought she'd stopped breathing. She was watching the woman playing Medea peel an orange. That was all. Rosa had written *she peels an orange through the following* and eight lines of Jason being generous about everyone's day, and the orange did more work than any of it, and Yael had known that for three years and was watching it be true in a room with actual light in it.

At thirty-one minutes Chen hit the six feet.

He started upstage at the bunks, three words — *you were nothing* — and came down, and arrived on *before me* close enough to the front row to be a problem, and he had not counted it. Yael saw him not count it. She saw Elena's hand stop over the light board because the amber wasn't cued yet and there was nothing to do but watch, and she saw Elena's head tilt very slightly to the left at exactly the angle Chen's head tilted when he was pleased with himself and refusing to show it, and the two of them stood there fifteen feet apart wearing the same face about the same moment, and Yael looked away.

She looked at the floor between her shoes for about a second and a half.

Then she stood up and said, "Hold," and the room exhaled, and she walked into the middle of it with her hands going.

"That's the show. That right there — Chen, that's the show, don't you dare improve it." She turned a full circle, taking in all of them. "Everyone. What you just did in the last ninety seconds is what we've been paying rent for. The reason it worked is nobody was selling it, so if I see anybody *deliver* that tomorrow I will cut the scene and we'll do it as a radio play." She put the glasses on. "Thank you. That was real work. Fifteen minutes, and then act two, and I'm cutting the chorus transition, so Elena, bring the book and something to cross things out with."

"Copy." Elena was already writing. "You want the four minutes or the six."

"Six."

Elena's pen stopped. "Six is the transition and the reprise."

"Six," Yael said, level. "You've been right since October. Take the whole thing."

Elena looked at her for a moment — one of the few people in the building permitted to — and then wrote it down, and said, "I'll re-plot the amber," and went, and Yael let out a breath nobody heard.

She came off the floor and stopped by the props table, where Jordan's phone was face-up and covered in time stamps, and she did not reach for it.

"Read them to me." The glasses came off. "Not what you felt. Just the numbers. I want to know where the play got you and I'd rather hear it from someone who's never read it."

**Jordan** (turn 19):
*I pick up my phone, a bit flustered. I hadn't expected her to ask.* "Okay, uh... at 9:15, when she said 'you're all just standing in a play.' And then at 22:30, with Okafor about the bread. And then, um... 31:00, when Chen did the six feet." *I look at her, a little hesitant.* "And then again at the very end, when you said 'the reason it worked is nobody was selling it'."

**Director Yael Mendez** (turn 20):
Yael did not say anything for a moment. She stood with the glasses in her fist and her head tipped very slightly back, the way she did when she was doing arithmetic she didn't like.

"Say them again."

Jordan said them again.

"Nine fifteen. Twenty-two thirty. Thirty-one. And the end." She nodded slowly. "Do you know what those four things have in common."

She didn't wait.

"I'm in all of them." Very quiet now. "Every single one. That's me stopping the scene, that's me talking to Tommy about bread, that's me giving a note to Chen four hours ago that he executed, and that's me making a speech. You sat through forty minutes of Rosa Delgado's play and the four times you looked at your phone, you were watching the director." The glasses went on, then straight off again. "That's not a compliment. I want to be extremely clear that that is not a compliment, and I'd appreciate it if you didn't hear it as one."

Behind her the room was dispersing toward the coffee that Anya should not touch. Tommy was moving the bread to the bench.

"Ask me what happened at twenty-six."

She turned and pointed out at the marked floor, at a chalk square near the stove flat.

"At around twenty-six minutes the woman playing Medea peels an orange. It's in the text — *she peels an orange through the following* — and Jason has eight lines about how generous he's being with everybody's morning, and she takes the peel off in one piece, and she doesn't eat it. She puts it down. That is the best ninety seconds in the first act. It's better than the knife. Rosa wrote it in 2019 and I have been waiting three years to see it in a room with real light in it and I sat there like a stone and watched it be true." A pause. "And you didn't clock it. Which means either you weren't paying attention — and you were, you're annoyingly good at this — or it isn't landing, and the reason it isn't landing is that I've built a production loud enough to stand in front of it."

She looked at the chair, the only chair, still sitting at the edge of the floor where she'd left it.

"So. Two options. One is I stop stopping. I don't say *hold* for the rest of the week, I let the run run, and I sit in the back where nobody can see me and find out what the play does when I'm not conducting it. Which I hate. Which means it's probably correct." A very dry beat. "The other is I've directed a memorial instead of a play, in which case Rosa is currently somewhere being vindicated about the building being overhead."

She picked up her glasses chain, found she was already holding the glasses, and put them on with something like irritation at herself.
